title: It’s Never Too Early to Start Planning for the Next Two Solar Eclipses
gist: Following the August 12 total solar eclipse, two more events in the 'Iberian eclipse trio' remain: an August 2, 2027 total eclipse with 6 minutes 23 seconds of totality — the longest in 100 years — crossing southern Spain, North Africa (peaking over Egypt's Thebes) and the Arabian Peninsula, and a January 26, 2028 annular 'ring of fire' eclipse running from Ecuador and Peru through Brazil to Portugal and Spain. Spain is the only European country in the 2027 path of totality, concentrating European eclipse tourism demand into a single destination.

insights.claim: The total solar eclipse of August 2, 2027 will hide the sun for 6 minutes and 23 seconds at peak, nearly three times the roughly 2 minutes 18 seconds of totality delivered by the August 12 eclipse, making it the longest total eclipse in 100 years.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: A once-per-century duration is the kind of scarcity that drives premium pricing in tour packages, hotel rates and charter capacity along the path — book and price exposure roughly 12-18 months ahead.
insights.locator: On August 2, 2027, one of the longest total solar eclipses

insights.claim: Spain will be the only European country from which the total phase of the 2027 eclipse can be observed, aside from the UK overseas territory of Gibraltar, concentrating the entire European totality market into a single national destination.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Geographic exclusivity means southern Spanish hospitality, rail and airport capacity absorbs continent-wide demand on a single date — a measurable one-day RevPAR and traffic spike for Andalusian operators.
insights.locator: Spain will be the only European country

insights.claim: The 2027 path of totality runs from southern Spain and northern Africa through Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, then Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Somalia — a corridor spanning countries with widely divergent tourism infrastructure and travel-security profiles.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Only a subset of the path is practically bookable for Western travelers, pushing demand disproportionately onto Spain, Morocco, Egypt and Saudi Arabia and inflating pricing power there.
insights.locator: A narrow band across the planet

insights.claim: Egypt will see both the peak and the longest duration of the 2027 eclipse, with the moon's shadow falling over ancient Thebes — the temples of Karnak and Luxor and the Valley of the Kings — while the Giza pyramids sit just outside totality and get only a partial eclipse.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: The overlap of maximum totality with Egypt's highest-value heritage sites is an unusually strong tourism catalyst for Luxor specifically, while Cairo/Giza operators miss the premium event.
insights.locator: Egypt will see both the peak of the eclipse

themes.theme: 2028 annular event and the Iberian trio

insights.claim: The January 26, 2028 annular eclipse will produce a visible ring of fire for 10 minutes and 27 seconds in Brazil, one of the longest annular eclipses of the century, along a path running from Ecuador and Peru across Brazil and the Atlantic to Portugal and Spain.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: A second cross-Atlantic event 18 months after 2027 extends the eclipse-tourism cycle into South America, spreading demand across two continents and two booking seasons.
insights.locator: The third eclipse in the series will occur on January 26, 2028

insights.claim: In Spanish cities including Seville, Córdoba, Albacete and Valencia the 2028 ring of fire will last about seven minutes and appear very close to the horizon shortly before sunset, a configuration described as potentially very photogenic.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Low-horizon sunset framing maximizes viral image potential, which historically drives the last-minute surge in domestic travel and camera/optics accessory sales.
insights.locator: Spain will experience a shorter but potentially very photogenic version

insights.claim: Europe is entering what the article calls a mini golden age of eclipses, with the 'Iberian eclipse trio' having two of three events still to come after August 12, giving destination marketers a multi-year rather than single-date planning horizon.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: A clustered multi-event sequence justifies durable capacity investment (viewing sites, transport, accommodation) rather than the one-off surge economics of a single eclipse.
insights.quote: the mini golden age of eclipses in Europe is just beginning
insights.locator: The total solar eclipse on August 12
